61153739.title: Outlive: The Science & Art of Longevity
61153739.author: Peter Attia
61153739.text: Peter Attia argues for approaching long-term health before serious disease becomes established, with the aim of preserving the ability to live well as well as living longer. Written with Bill Gifford, the book examines aging, major chronic diseases, and the relationship between prevention and medical treatment. Exercise, nutrition, sleep, and emotional well-being form part of Attia's proposed approach. He encourages readers to think about individual risks and the future capacities they hope to maintain. The book combines explanations of health research with the author's perspective on the limits of conventional care and the possibilities of a more proactive model.

1885.title: Pride and Prejudice
1885.author: Jane Austen
1885.text: Elizabeth Bennet lives in a family whose daughters face serious pressure to marry securely. When the wealthy, reserved Mr. Darcy enters her social world, first impressions harden into judgments that neither finds easy to reconsider. Jane Austen follows courtship through visits, conversations, and family embarrassments, revealing how affection is entangled with money and social position. Elizabeth's independence and wit give the story its lively center, but intelligence does not make her immune to misreading others. The novel examines the work of knowing oneself and another person within a society highly practiced at judging appearances.

226573163.title: The Gales of November: The Untold Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald
226573163.author: John U. Bacon
226573163.text: John U. Bacon examines the loss of the Edmund Fitzgerald through the history of Great Lakes shipping and the lives of the men aboard it. The freighter sank on Lake Superior during a November 1975 storm, leaving families and communities to confront a disaster without survivors. Drawing on interviews with relatives, friends, and former crewmates, Bacon places the final voyage within the working world that supported American industry. He considers possible causes alongside the human aftermath. The book seeks to recover individual lives behind a familiar maritime story while acknowledging the uncertainties surrounding the ship's last hours.

204274500.title: Resistance Money

They explain its origins and operation before considering privacy, censorship, monetary policy, access to finance, and energy use. Their argument asks how a monetary system should be judged when people face very different institutions and constraints. The authors defend Bitcoin's potential benefits while addressing objections and costs, including environmental concerns. Intended for readers with varied levels of technical knowledge, the book frames its subject as a question about money, power, and human freedom rather than price alone.

8935689.title: Consider Phlebas (Culture, #1)

Banks introduces the Culture through a space adventure that questions the moral language of war and the costs borne by individuals inside it. The search combines strange worlds and uncertain alliances with the tension between personal conviction and vast political forces.

43263680.title: Ninth House (Ninth House Trilogy, #1)
43263680.author: Leigh Bardugo
43263680.text: Alex Stern arrives at Yale with a past that makes her an unlikely undergraduate and an opportunity she does not fully understand. Her admission comes with a hidden assignment: observing the university's secret societies, whose privileges extend into forbidden magic. Having survived a violent, troubled life outside elite institutions, Alex must navigate a new world where status and occult power reinforce each other. Leigh Bardugo sets supernatural danger among familiar academic rituals and ambitious people. The novel follows an outsider trying to understand what her benefactors want, while discovering that the institution offering a fresh start also harbors threats.

58233.title: From Dawn to Decadence: 500 Years of Western Cultural Life, 1500 to the Present
58233.author: Jacques Barzun
58233.text: Jacques Barzun surveys five centuries of Western cultural life, tracing connections among ideas, institutions, and the people who changed them. Beginning with the Renaissance and Reformation, his narrative ranges across artistic, intellectual, religious, and political developments rather than treating each field as an isolated history. Individual portraits and recurring themes give shape to a vast period of change. Barzun interprets the modern era as having its own trajectory, including creative achievements and signs of exhaustion. The book is both a synthesis of cultural history and a sustained personal argument about how the inheritance of the past has reached the present.

193755.title: The Diving Bell and the Butterfly: A Memoir of Life in Death
193755.author: Jean-Dominique Bauby
193755.text: After a severe stroke, French magazine editor Jean-Dominique Bauby finds himself almost completely unable to move, while his mind remains active. By blinking one eye to select letters, he composes an account of life within that extraordinary confinement. Memories, imagined journeys, humor, and frustration move alongside encounters with family and the daily realities of dependence. The memoir explores the gap between what a body can express and what a person continues to experience. Bauby's voice makes room for wit as well as grief, turning painstaking communication into a record of identity, longing, and the persistence of an inner world.

438452.title: The Long Ships

Bengtsson turns the violence and uncertainty of the Viking age into a broad historical tale filled with dry humor. Captivity, travel, feuds, and political intrigue repeatedly change Orm's circumstances. 62050269.title: A Brief History of Intelligence: Evolution, AI, and the Five Breakthroughs That Made Our Brains

He connects evolutionary history and neuroscience with questions raised by artificial intelligence, asking why machines can excel at some tasks while struggling with abilities that seem ordinary in living creatures. The book uses the past to illuminate both the strengths and limitations of contemporary AI. Its central proposal is that understanding how minds developed can offer useful ideas for building artificial systems. Bennett presents a broad framework for exploring intelligence across biological and technological forms.

150247395.title: The Tainted Cup (Ana and Din Mysteries, #1)
150247395.author: Robert Jackson Bennett

The case falls to Ana Dolabra, an eccentric detective, and her new assistant Dinios Kol, whose altered abilities make him a valuable partner. 174354.title: Over the Edge of the World: Magellan's Terrifying Circumnavigation of the Globe
174354.author: Laurence Bergreen
174354.text: Laurence Bergreen recounts the sixteenth-century expedition led by Ferdinand Magellan that set out to find a passage across the globe. The voyage becomes an ordeal of uncertain navigation, conflict, hunger, and encounters far beyond the sailors' familiar world. Drawing on firsthand accounts, Bergreen connects the ambitions behind the expedition with the difficult human experience of carrying them out. The story considers the courage and violence bound together in the era of European maritime expansion. Its focus is a journey that transformed geographic understanding while exposing the limits of leadership, endurance, and the knowledge on which the travelers depended.

54143.title: Lost City of the Incas

54143.text: Hiram Bingham recounts his travels in Peru and the search that brought him to Machu Picchu in 1911. The book combines an explorer's experience of the landscape with his effort to interpret surviving buildings and traces of the Inca past. It records the perspective of an early twentieth-century investigator, including the assumptions that shaped his search. The result is a personal account of exploration and archaeological interpretation, centered on a place whose significance exceeded Bingham's original expectations.

52199304.title: The World for Sale: Money, Power and the Traders Who Barter the Earth’s Resources
52199304.author: Javier Blas
52199304.text: Javier Blas and Jack Farchy investigate the commodity traders who connect the world's sources of oil, metals, and food with the markets that depend on them. These businesses often operate far from public attention while negotiating with governments, financing deals, and profiting from upheaval. The authors trace how individual traders and trading houses acquired influence over the movement of essential resources. Their reporting links commercial ambition to political consequences, showing why apparently obscure transactions can matter to entire countries. The book examines a part of globalization where enormous fortunes, practical necessity, and questions of accountability repeatedly meet.

75812.title: The Closing of the American Mind
75812.author: Allan Bloom
75812.text: Allan Bloom argues that problems in American public life are connected to a deeper crisis in intellectual culture and higher education. Drawing on his perspective as a teacher and political philosopher, he questions whether universities encourage the curiosity and serious inquiry they are meant to cultivate. His discussion places students' experiences alongside larger questions about philosophy, cultural inheritance, and the purposes of education. The book presents a provocative interpretation of the relationship between learning and democratic society. Its concern is not simply what students know, but what aspirations and habits of mind an education makes available to them.

sources.title: The Closing of the American Mind — Simon & Schuster

1471204.title: Developing Talent in Young People
1471204.author: Benjamin S. Bloom
1471204.text: Benjamin Bloom and his collaborators investigate how exceptional ability develops through a study of highly accomplished people across several fields. Musicians, sculptors, athletes, mathematicians, and research neurologists provide different settings in which to examine learning over time. The book considers the influence of home life, the phases of training, and the sustained commitment involved in reaching a high level of achievement. Individual accounts sit beside broader comparisons across the study. Its focus is the process by which young people develop their abilities, inviting attention to the circumstances and experiences surrounding talent rather than treating excellence as an unexplained gift.

sources.title: Developing Talent in Young People — Penguin Random House

1153633.title: The Mind of Napoleon: A Selection of His Written and Spoken Words
1153633.author: Napoléon Bonaparte
1153633.text: Edited and translated by J. Christopher Herold, this selection brings together Napoleon's written and spoken reflections on subjects extending well beyond the battlefield. The material is organized around themes including government, law, religion, education, the arts, human character, and the conduct of war. It also includes Napoleon's reflections on his own career, placing public ambitions beside his view of himself. The collection offers access to the language and judgments of a historical ruler through an editor's arrangement of source material. Readers encounter a portrait assembled from statements, with the distinction between self-presentation and independent historical assessment left visible.

sources.title: The Mind of Napoleon — Columbia University Press / De Gruyter Brill

49750306.title: Driving Digital Transformation through Data and AI: A Practical Guide to Delivering Data Science and Machine Learning Products
49750306.author: Alexander Borek
49750306.text: Alexander Borek and Nadine Prill examine why promising data and machine learning projects often remain isolated experiments instead of becoming useful business products. Their guide connects product strategy with organizational structure, delivery processes, architecture, and governance. It considers how executives can coordinate competing needs, develop a portfolio of data products, and support teams responsible for putting them into operation. Case studies, templates, and discussion of common mistakes accompany the framework. The book treats digital transformation as a change in how an organization works, requiring the alignment of technology, people, and business priorities around products that can be delivered at scale.

17961.title: Collected Fictions
17961.author: Jorge Luis Borges
17961.text: Jorge Luis Borges turns short fiction into a place where ideas become adventures and familiar forms open onto unsettling possibilities. Across this collection, dreams, mirrors, labyrinths, invented books, and uncertain identities recur alongside duels and the figures of Argentine life. Detective stories become philosophical puzzles, while seemingly scholarly accounts lead into imagined worlds. The volume spans his fiction across decades, allowing recurring concerns to appear in different shapes and scales. Its stories invite readers to question the stability of reality and the authority of narration, often using a small, precisely described invention to suggest something immeasurably larger.

sources.title: Collected Fictions — Penguin Random House

17961.reviewNotes: Same collected work; no catalog ISBN. Overview of motifs and range, with no individual story resolutions or unsupported translation claim.

5787.title: The Aleph and Other Stories
5787.author: Jorge Luis Borges
5787.text: In these stories, Jorge Luis Borges joins philosophical speculation to vivid situations involving faith, violence, revenge, and identity. Characters facing imprisonment, accusation, or death become the center of puzzles that disturb ordinary assumptions about meaning and reality. The collection ranges across different places and historical settings while retaining an intimate interest in the minds inhabiting them. Brief pieces from The Maker extend the inquiry into imagination and the sense of self. The result is a set of compact fictions in which a personal obsession or strange encounter can reveal the instability of apparently secure ideas about the world.

sources.title: The Aleph and Other Stories — Penguin Random House

61685983.title: Morning After the Revolution: Dispatches from the Wrong Side of History
61685983.author: Nellie Bowles
61685983.text: Nellie Bowles examines progressive political culture through reporting and her own experience of becoming skeptical of a movement she had supported. Visiting activist settings and reflecting on newsroom life, she questions whether the practices she encounters achieve their stated aims. Her accounts use satire and personal observation to explore the pressures of belonging, dissent, and moral certainty within influential institutions. The book presents a critical perspective on a particular moment in American public life, with Bowles positioning herself as both former participant and observer. Its emphasis is on the distance she perceives between political intentions and their everyday expression.

sources.title: Morning After the Revolution — Penguin Random House

61685983.reviewNotes: Exact catalog ISBN. Political assessments explicitly attributed to Bowles; publisher's inflammatory promotional judgments not adopted as fact.

34523114.title: Island of the Blue Foxes: Disaster and Triumph on the World's Greatest Scientific Expedition
34523114.author: Stephen R. Bown
34523114.text: Stephen Bown recounts the Great Northern Expedition, an immense Russian undertaking that carried people and supplies across Siberia before sending ships toward North America. Vitus Bering and naturalist Georg Steller stand among the figures attempting to turn scientific and geographic ambitions into discoveries. The effort's scale creates extraordinary logistical difficulties, while rivalries, weather, and isolation make the voyage increasingly precarious. A remote island becomes the setting for a struggle to endure the consequences of disaster. The book combines the history of exploration with the experiences of people whose plans for knowledge and achievement were tested by conditions beyond their control.

sources.title: Island of the Blue Foxes — Stephen R. Bown

13587148.title: The Last Viking: The Life of Roald Amundsen (A Merloyd Lawrence Book)
13587148.author: Stephen R. Bown
13587148.text: Stephen Bown follows Roald Amundsen through a career devoted to the most demanding journeys of the polar world. The biography examines the preparation, technical skill, and determination behind his expeditions, while also considering the complicated person who pursued them. Relationships with companions, financial pressures, rivalry, and public celebrity accompany the geographic achievements. Bown draws on archival material to place Amundsen within an era when exploration was becoming entangled with new technology and publicity. The book brings the practical work of reaching difficult places together with the ambitions and private conflicts that made the explorer's life more than a sequence of triumphs.

sources.title: The Last Viking — Stephen R. Bown

103430.title: The Structures of Everyday Life: Civilization and Capitalism 15th-18th Century, Volume 1
103430.author: Fernand Braudel
103430.text: Fernand Braudel approaches the history of capitalism by examining the material conditions of everyday life before industrialization. This first volume considers food, clothing, housing, population, family life, technology, money, and the growth of towns. Rather than beginning with famous rulers or individual commercial successes, it looks at the ordinary necessities and constraints within which people acted. The scale extends across societies, showing how basic arrangements of living formed a foundation for economic activity. Braudel brings apparently mundane details into a broad historical inquiry, asking what daily life made possible and what limits it placed on change.

sources.title: The Structures of Everyday Life — publisher summary in WorldCat

103430.reviewNotes: Explicitly publisher-provided summary in OCLC record for 1992 UC Press same volume; catalog Harper edition differs. Synopsis limited to Volume I, not later volumes' market analysis.

116965815.title: Finding Endurance: Shackleton, My Father and a World Without End
116965815.author: Darrel Bristow-Bovey
116965815.text: The discovery of the wreck of Endurance prompts Darrel Bristow-Bovey to return to Shackleton's expedition and to his own long fascination with it. He revisits the voyage's hardship and survival while asking why a ship lost in the Antarctic can still move people far removed from polar exploration. His father's stories become part of a more personal inquiry into memory, admiration, and the bonds between parents and children. Combining expedition history with reflection, the book considers the strength imperfect people can show in desperate circumstances and the ways a story from the past can restore a sense of possibility.

sources.title: Finding Endurance — Icon Books

116965815.reviewNotes: Publisher ebook listing supports same work; catalog format differs. Father's claimed participation treated as family story, not independently verified history.

31253736.title: The Fifth Trimester: The Working Mom's Guide to Style, Sanity, and Big Success After Baby
31253736.author: Lauren Smith Brody
31253736.text: Lauren Smith Brody focuses on the transition from maternity leave back to paid work, a period that can bring unfamiliar practical and emotional demands. Drawing on the experiences of hundreds of mothers, she considers childcare, workplace conversations, feeding logistics, sleep disruption, and the effort to recover professional confidence. The guide treats returning to work as its own stage of adjustment, with different arrangements possible for different families. Advice and personal accounts aim to make the experience less isolating. The book's central concern is how women can navigate the collision of new responsibilities while seeking support and a workable daily life.

sources.title: The Fifth Trimester — Penguin Random House

31253736.reviewNotes: Publisher description and author interview read; same work, different current format. No medical efficacy or legal-entitlement claims included.

20898092.title: Jane Eyre
20898092.author: Charlotte Brontë
20898092.text: After a childhood marked by harsh treatment, Jane Eyre seeks independence through work as a governess. Her position in the household of the enigmatic Mr. Rochester offers both a new world and a powerful emotional attachment, but secrets complicate what seems possible between them. Charlotte Brontë gives Jane a searching, insistent voice as she weighs love against self-respect and conviction. The novel joins Gothic mystery to a young woman's effort to determine the terms of her own life. Its drama grows from the tension between the security she longs for and the principles she refuses to abandon.

sources.title: Jane Eyre — Penguin Random House

112974860.title: How to Know a Person: The Art of Seeing Others Deeply and Being Deeply Seen
112974860.author: David  Brooks
112974860.text: David Brooks explores the attention and conversational habits involved in understanding another person beyond a first impression. Drawing on ideas from psychology, the humanities, and other fields, he asks how people can listen well, recognize individual stories, and help others feel valued. The book connects these everyday encounters with wider concerns about isolation, hostility, and misunderstanding. Its practical focus is the effort required to see someone as a complex individual rather than a familiar category. Brooks presents human connection as a skill that can be developed, with consequences for relationships at home, at work, and in public life.

sources.title: How to Know a Person — Penguin Random House

112974860.reviewNotes: Same work; current paperback default differs from catalog hardcover. Author's approach described without promising psychological outcomes.

35820369.title: The Rise and Fall of the Dinosaurs: A New History of a Lost World
35820369.author: Steve Brusatte
35820369.text: Steve Brusatte traces the dinosaur story from early origins through the long period when these animals dominated terrestrial ecosystems and into the catastrophe that ended that dominance. Fossil discoveries provide the evidence for an account of changing bodies, environments, and ways of life. Alongside the deep history, Brusatte introduces the people and fieldwork behind modern paleontology, including episodes from his own research. The book connects familiar prehistoric animals with the methods used to understand them, showing how new finds can transform old assumptions. Its narrative combines a vanished world's history with the continuing scientific work of reconstructing it.

sources.title: The Rise and Fall of the Dinosaurs — Pan Macmillan

1377703.title: The Invention That Changed the World
1377703.author: Robert Buderi
1377703.text: Robert Buderi tells the story of radar as both a wartime invention and a source of lasting technological change. The narrative follows the people whose research and engineering turned a scientific possibility into an instrument with major consequences during the Second World War. Their work, including the effort centered on a secret laboratory at MIT, becomes part of a broader account of innovation under extraordinary pressure. Buderi then considers the technological legacy that followed the war. The book places inventors and institutions behind a familiar technology, connecting urgent military problems with developments that reached far beyond their original purpose.

sources.title: The Invention That Changed the World — Simon & Schuster

1377703.reviewNotes: Publisher matches catalog ISBN. Avoids sole-cause claim that radar alone won WWII; subject and broad narrative scope only.

13543121.title: Between Two Fires
13543121.author: Christopher Buehlman
13543121.text: In plague-stricken France in 1348, a disgraced knight named Thomas encounters a young girl who claims the catastrophe has a supernatural cause. She persuades him to escort her toward Avignon, turning a journey through a devastated country into an encounter with forces that threaten more than human life. Thomas's damaged faith and violent past accompany him through a landscape of suffering and uncanny danger. Christopher Buehlman blends medieval horror with questions of mercy, belief, and redemption. The novel places a vulnerable partnership within an apocalyptic struggle, leaving its travelers uncertain about what they can trust or hope to save.

sources.title: Between Two Fires — Tor Nightfire / Macmillan

207746.title: The Oxford Book of English Short Stories (Oxford Books of Prose)
207746.author: A.S. Byatt
207746.text: A. S. Byatt selects English short stories from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to display the form's variety rather than force it into a single pattern. Familiar authors appear beside less expected choices, with social observation, comedy, ghost stories, fantasy, and other approaches sharing the collection. Some pieces stay close to recognizable daily life; others unsettle the reader's expectations about where a story can lead. The anthology's connections emerge through contrasts in tone, subject, and technique. Byatt's selection offers a reading journey across different kinds of imagination, emphasizing the surprise and concentration possible within a short work.

sources.title: The Oxford Book of English Short Stories — Oxford University Press

207746.reviewNotes: Publisher regional page read; same 37-story anthology, different reprint ISBN. Byatt identified as editor, no claim she authored collected stories.

35513.title: A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living
35513.author: Joseph Campbell
35513.text: This collection brings together Joseph Campbell's reflections on how mythology intersects with individual experience and the choices involved in living. Drawing from a seminar at the Esalen Institute as well as lectures and published work, it presents observations in an accessible, conversational form. Campbell considers the inner significance of stories and the ways inherited images can inform a person's understanding of life. The book offers a selection of his thought rather than a single continuous argument or systematic survey of world mythology. Its emphasis is the relationship between imagination, personal discovery, and the effort to find meaning in ordinary experience.

sources.title: A Joseph Campbell Companion — Joseph Campbell Foundation

10266902.title: Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids: Why Being a Great Parent Is Less Work and More Fun Than You Think
10266902.author: Bryan Caplan
10266902.text: Bryan Caplan challenges the assumption that good parenting requires ever more intensive effort to shape children's futures. Drawing on his interpretation of research involving twins and adoption, he argues that parents may overestimate their influence on many long-term outcomes. From that premise, he explores how reducing unnecessary pressure could make family life more enjoyable and affect decisions about having children. The book combines an economist's perspective with an argument about the costs people associate with parenthood. Caplan asks readers to reconsider which sacrifices matter, while making a provocative case for a less anxious approach to raising a family.

sources.title: Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids — Basic Books / Hachette

18554985.title: The Systems View of Life: A Unifying Vision
18554985.author: Fritjof Capra
18554985.text: Fritjof Capra and Pier Luigi Luisi bring together scientific ideas that understand living things through relationships, networks, and patterns of organization. The book traces the development of systems thinking and explains concepts concerning how life maintains and organizes itself. Its scope moves across biology and other disciplines, connecting the study of living systems with questions about society. The authors also consider implications for health, management, and ecological and economic problems. Intended as an introduction for students and other interested readers, the work presents a unified framework for thinking about life as interconnected processes rather than an assembly of isolated parts.

13049569.title: The Passage of Power (The Years of Lyndon Johnson, #4)
13049569.author: Robert A. Caro
13049569.text: Robert Caro follows Lyndon Johnson from his command of the Senate through the frustrations of the vice presidency and into the presidency after John Kennedy's assassination. Covering 1958 to 1964, this volume examines the political maneuvers, personal tensions, and institutional knowledge that shaped Johnson's passage between sharply different levels of authority. Caro gives particular attention to the rapid consolidation of presidential power during a national crisis. The account connects biography with an inquiry into what political skill can accomplish when circumstances change. It is a study of ambition and opportunity at a pivotal stage of Johnson's career.

189989.title: Finite and Infinite Games: A Vision of Life as Play and Possibility
189989.author: James P. Carse
189989.text: James Carse begins with a distinction between contests played to secure a result and forms of play whose purpose is to remain open and continue. He uses that contrast to explore ambitions, relationships, cultural life, and the ways people understand their place in the world. Winning, status, and fixed boundaries belong to one orientation; ongoing possibility and changing participation characterize the other. The book develops its philosophical inquiry through short, reflective propositions rather than a conventional practical manual. It asks what changes when life is approached as participation in an unfolding activity instead of a competition that must be concluded.

108490.title: The Conquest of New Spain
108490.author: Bernal Díaz del Castillo
108490.text: Bernal Díaz del Castillo recounts the Spanish conquest of Mexico from the perspective of a soldier who served under Hernán Cortés. His narrative describes encounters with the people and cities of the region, the pursuit of wealth, reversals in the campaign, and the struggle over the Aztec capital. The detail of a participant's recollection gives the account its distinctive immediacy, while also making its viewpoint essential to understanding it. Read as a historical source, the work reveals both events and the way a conqueror remembered them, offering evidence that must be considered alongside the experiences his position could not fully represent.

18077903.title: Creativity, Inc.: Overcoming the Unseen Forces That Stand in the Way of True Inspiration
18077903.author: Ed Catmull
18077903.text: Ed Catmull, writing with Amy Wallace, reflects on building Pixar and the organizational conditions that allow creative people to do difficult work together. The narrative connects the development of computer animation with management questions about communication, trust, risk, and mistakes. Catmull argues that protecting creativity requires active attention to the barriers organizations create, including habits that prevent problems from being discussed openly. Experiences from filmmaking provide a setting for broader lessons about leading talented teams. The book examines the continuing work of maintaining a creative culture, treating successful projects as products of collective effort rather than isolated flashes of inspiration.

22309541.title: The Procurement Value Proposition: The Rise of Supply Management
22309541.author: Gerard Chick
22309541.text: Gerard Chick and Robert Handfield examine how procurement can contribute to a business beyond the immediate task of reducing purchase costs. They place supply management within changes in technology, economic conditions, sustainability, and organizational expectations. The discussion considers strategy, structure, responsibilities, and the skills required as procurement becomes a more central business function. Case studies and observations from practitioners show organizations adapting their approaches in different settings. The book's central argument is that procurement's value depends on understanding wider business needs and changing supply relationships, making its development a question of organizational capability as well as purchasing efficiency.

22155.title: Let My People Go Surfing: The Education of a Reluctant Businessman
22155.author: Yvon Chouinard
22155.text: Yvon Chouinard traces the unlikely path from climbing enthusiast and equipment maker to founder of Patagonia. His account connects outdoor adventure with decisions about product quality, employees, and the environmental costs of business. Rather than separating commercial success from personal values, he describes a company intended to reflect the life its founder wanted to lead. Autobiography gives way to a statement of business principles, asking what responsible production and consumption might require. The book presents Chouinard's own experiment in running a company while remaining answerable to the natural places that inspired it.

13425570.title: How Will You Measure Your Life?
13425570.author: Clayton M. Christensen
13425570.text: Clayton Christensen, with James Allworth and Karen Dillon, applies ideas from management research to questions about a satisfying life. The book considers why professional achievement may fail to provide meaning, how commitments to family and friendship can be neglected, and how small ethical compromises accumulate. Business examples become tools for examining motivation, long-term choices, and the gap between stated priorities and daily behavior. Instead of prescribing a single career or definition of success, the authors encourage readers to develop principles for making decisions and judging whether their lives reflect what they value.

2615.title: The Innovator's Dilemma: The Revolutionary Book that Will Change the Way You Do Business
2615.author: Clayton M. Christensen
2615.text: Why can well-managed companies lose their position when a new technology arrives? Clayton Christensen argues that the practices supporting established businesses can also make them vulnerable. Attention to profitable customers and familiar measures of performance may discourage investment in initially modest markets that later become important. Drawing on cases of corporate success and failure, he develops the idea of disruptive innovation and examines the management choices it presents. The book asks leaders to recognize when conventional rules no longer fit, and to consider how new activities can develop without being constrained by an existing business.

2618.text: Clayton Christensen and Michael Raynor turn from explaining why established companies stumble to considering how businesses can create new growth. Building on the theory of disruptive innovation, they examine the processes and strategic decisions that make promising opportunities easier to identify and develop. Their account treats innovation as something managers can study and organize, rather than a matter of waiting for exceptional ideas. Examples across industries support an approach that adapts choices to circumstances. The book addresses the challenge of nurturing new businesses while avoiding assumptions inherited from a company's existing sources of success.

18730716.title: The Son Also Rises: Surnames and the History of Social Mobility
18730716.author: Gregory Clark
18730716.text: Gregory Clark uses surnames to investigate how social standing persists across generations. Comparing families in different countries and historical periods, he argues that movement between social ranks is slower than many conventional estimates suggest. His analysis challenges optimistic accounts of modern mobility and questions how much institutions and policy can change inherited patterns. The book connects an unusual historical method with debates about opportunity, inequality, and the rewards society assigns to success. Its conclusions are presented as Clark's interpretation of the evidence, including his case for limiting the consequences of unequal social positions.

677285.title: Ignition!: An informal history of liquid rocket propellants
677285.author: John Drury Clark
677285.text: John Drury Clark recounts the search for liquid rocket propellants from the perspective of a chemist who took part in it. Rival laboratories pursue mixtures powerful enough for demanding missions while confronting instability, hazardous substances, and unpredictable experiments. Technical explanations sit beside stories about the personalities and working habits of the researchers involved. The result combines scientific history with an irreverent professional memoir, showing how practical engineering advances emerged through trial, argument, and failure. Its subject is the difficult development of usable rocket fuels, and the people whose ingenuity and persistence made that work possible.

60704017.title: The Fiscal Theory of the Price Level
60704017.author: John H. Cochrane
60704017.text: John Cochrane develops an account of inflation centered on government debt and expectations about future public finances. In this framework, the price level adjusts in relation to the value people assign to the government's promised fiscal backing. He connects that argument to models of interest-rate policy, historical episodes, and questions about monetary institutions. The book moves from basic theoretical cases toward complications needed for practical analysis, including changing expectations and prices that adjust gradually. It presents fiscal theory as a research framework for understanding inflation, rather than treating central-bank decisions in isolation from government budgets.

30646587.title: The Simple Path to Wealth: Your Road Map to Financial Independence and a Rich, Free Life
30646587.author: J.L. Collins
30646587.text: J. L. Collins presents financial independence as a way to gain greater control over one's time and choices. His approach emphasizes spending less than earnings, avoiding burdensome debt, and keeping investment decisions understandable. Personal stories and plain explanations challenge the notion that managing money must involve constant activity or complicated expertise. The book links financial habits to the kind of life they are meant to support, asking readers to think beyond consumption or status. It offers Collins's philosophy for building and using wealth, with simplicity and patience at the center of that philosophy.

56614591.title: Trauma: The Invisible Epidemic: How Trauma Works and How We Can Heal From It
56614591.author: Paul Conti
56614591.text: Psychiatrist Paul Conti examines how trauma can shape emotions, memory, decisions, and relationships even when its effects are difficult to recognize. He links individual experiences with family patterns and wider social conditions, arguing that hidden suffering deserves more attention and understanding. The book combines explanation with discussion of responses to fear and distress, presenting compassion as part of the process of recovery. Conti also asks how communities might reduce the conditions that perpetuate trauma. His account is an accessible statement of his clinical perspective, focused on recognizing patterns and making healing more conceivable.

125937631.title: Material World: The Six Raw Materials That Shape Modern Civilization
125937631.author: Ed Conway
125937631.text: Ed Conway follows six materials that support modern civilization: sand, salt, iron, copper, oil, and lithium. Visiting mines, factories, and other industrial sites, he traces the transformations that turn ordinary substances into technologies people depend on. The journey connects local labor and technical ingenuity with international supply chains, political competition, and environmental pressures. A world that appears increasingly digital emerges as deeply dependent on physical extraction and processing. Conway's account brings overlooked workers and processes into view, asking what the material foundations of everyday life reveal about both human achievement and future demands.

44644.title: Principle-Centered Leadership
44644.author: Stephen R. Covey
44644.text: Stephen Covey argues that effective leadership begins with the principles and habits of the person exercising it. He connects personal conduct with the way organizations develop trust, encourage talent, and respond to change. Questions about productivity and quality sit alongside questions about relationships and the balance between professional and family life. 75243.text: William Cronon examines Chicago's nineteenth-century growth through its changing relationship with the surrounding country. The city and its hinterland emerge as parts of one economic and ecological system, connected by the movement of resources, capital, and people. Urban expansion transforms distant landscapes, while those landscapes help make urban prosperity possible. By placing environmental change inside business and regional history, Cronon challenges an easy division between city and nature. His account shows how the rise of a commercial metropolis helped reshape American culture and territory, revealing connections that remain embedded in the modern world.

Plants, animals, and diseases helped transform environments in the temperate regions where European populations became established. He argues that these biological changes were central to the displacement of Indigenous peoples and to the creation of new agricultural societies. The study connects ecology with a long history of colonization, asking why expansion succeeded so decisively in some regions. Its central claim is that the consequences of empire cannot be understood through human intentions and military power alone.

Edited by Richard Crossman, the collection includes accounts by Arthur Koestler, Ignazio Silone, Richard Wright, André Gide, Louis Fischer, and Stephen Spender. Their different backgrounds reveal how political commitment could become entangled with moral aspiration, identity, and loyalty. The essays concentrate on the personal difficulty of recognizing a conflict between an ideal and the movement claiming to embody it. Together they form a record of intellectual disillusionment within the ideological struggles of the twentieth century.

Detective Barry Sutton investigates the disturbing phenomenon, while neuroscientist Helena Smith pursues research with implications she cannot yet fully understand. Their stories converge around a discovery that threatens the boundaries between memory, identity, and reality. Blake Crouch turns scientific possibility into a thriller about the desire to recover what has been lost and the dangers of changing experience itself. The mystery expands beyond individual minds, forcing its central characters to confront consequences that make familiar ideas about time increasingly difficult to trust.

The city depends on navigation, negotiation, and control of distant routes as much as on its unusual position in a lagoon. Crowley's history draws on accounts of the people caught in these contests, exploring how an enterprising trading community acquired an empire and how its dominance came under pressure.

Barry Crump follows an unlikely partnership between a Māori boy and a stubborn older man whose shared predicament gradually changes their relationship. Humor accompanies the dangers of life on the run, while the landscape tests their resourcefulness. The novel centers on survival, belonging, and the trust that can grow between outsiders.

18294553.text: Sam Daley-Harris challenges the feeling that ordinary citizens have little influence over public decisions. Drawing on his experience with organized advocacy, he describes how people can move from frustration or disengagement toward sustained participation. The book connects personal changes in confidence with collective efforts to address poverty and other public problems. Its emphasis is on learning to act with others, developing a voice, and treating democratic involvement as an ongoing practice. Daley-Harris offers a hopeful account of citizenship grounded in the belief that the distance between people and government can be reduced through deliberate effort.

His history connects environmental processes with markets, power, and the vulnerability of rural populations. George Mallory and his fellow climbers approach the mountain carrying experiences shaped by a conflict that had transformed their generation. Pacific navigation, Amazonian knowledge, and traditions from other regions reveal capacities that industrial societies may overlook. These lectures argue that cultural diversity is a store of imagination and practical understanding, not a collection of curiosities destined to disappear. Davis considers what is lost when languages and ways of life are threatened, and why their survival matters beyond the communities concerned. His remarkable appetite for learning creates problems that ordinary schooling cannot easily accommodate. Helen DeWitt follows their intellectual and emotional negotiations as Ludo begins his own search. The novel brings exuberant learning into contact with loneliness, parenthood, and the desire to find someone whose example might offer a meaningful way to live.

12187787.title: The Beginning of Infinity: Explanations That Transform the World

12187787.text: David Deutsch argues that progress depends on creating explanations, criticizing them, and replacing those that fail. Moving across science, philosophy, politics, and culture, he examines the conditions under which knowledge can grow and the habits that prevent it from doing so. His case for the possibility of continuing progress rests on human fallibility and the ability to solve problems through better understanding. The book links questions about the physical universe with questions about institutions and creativity. It offers an expansive argument that the limits people encounter need not always be permanent limits to what they can know.

A murder turns that idea into a reality he cannot master, drawing him into fear, guilt, and a tense encounter with investigation. Fyodor Dostoevsky places the reader close to his unstable reasoning while surrounding him with people whose suffering and loyalties challenge his self-image. The novel joins psychological suspense with questions about responsibility and the possibility of moral change. Its drama comes from the distance between an argument that seems convincing in isolation and the consequences of acting upon it.

Fyodor Dostoevsky uses this difficult voice to explore the contradictions of consciousness, the limits of rational explanations, and the ways people can participate in their own unhappiness. The short novel asks readers to listen closely to a speaker who resists sympathy even as he seeks an audience, exposing the tension between isolation and the need for human connection.

A crime draws those tensions into a public drama of accusation and judgment. Dostoevsky combines the movement of a mystery with arguments about belief, freedom, responsibility, and love.
